scenes.title: The unsent message
scenes.visual: Black hand cut from paper holds white rectangular phone; words HOW ARE YOU? appear and become scratches.

scenes.title: The weight of ordinary words
scenes.visual: Phone rectangle shrinks against enormous red field, text becomes tiny chalk dots.

scenes.title: What the song asks
scenes.visual: Huge hand-lettered ALFAAZ grows while thousands of microscopic letters dissolve.

scenes.title: The thesis
scenes.visual: A human profile carved from ink, second silhouette forms inside.

scenes.title: Change without permission
scenes.visual: Tea cup, red scarf and tiny story scraps orbit a simple silhouette.

scenes.title: The invisible new habit
scenes.visual: Thought line travels from protagonist to an absent outline; line becomes a path.

scenes.title: The changed self
scenes.visual: Layers of profile cutouts shift out of registration, revealing another contour.

scenes.title: A necessary question
scenes.visual: Two silhouettes share a shadow, then step into two distinct shadows.

scenes.title: A street can remember
scenes.visual: Black street lamps on red painted road; footprints overlay like cut-paper memories.

scenes.title: Ordinary places become sacred
scenes.visual: Bus stop morphs into cafe cup, then a tiny gramophone.

scenes.title: The world versus its meaning
scenes.visual: Flat red city folds into map of thin red thread around black cutouts.

scenes.title: Attention as generosity
scenes.visual: Eye sketched in charcoal becomes cup reflection; tiny gestures written round iris.

scenes.title: Uncertainty enters
scenes.visual: Two eyes on opposite sides of frame, one bright and one fading.

scenes.title: The silent screen
scenes.visual: Phone framed between giant hands, no notification; thought bubbles misalign.

scenes.title: The fear beneath distance
scenes.visual: Two hand-drawn portraits; one portrait fades while the paper around it remains.

scenes.title: Other minds remain other
scenes.visual: Black oval opens into a second independent landscape with different marks.

scenes.title: Care without possession
scenes.visual: Two silhouettes face each other across narrow blank paper, no forced merge.

scenes.title: What we knew how to give
scenes.visual: Ink hand holds imperfectly drawn heart; lines repaired with white pencil.

scenes.title: Feeling versus practice
scenes.visual: Three ordinary hands: offering tea, holding door, placing note.

scenes.title: Fromm and action
scenes.visual: A painted red heart transforms into hands performing helpful actions.

scenes.title: The limit of sincerity
scenes.visual: Giant speaking mouth collapses, replaced by listening ear and quiet open hand.

scenes.title: Language is finite
scenes.visual: Letters burst outward from mouth into vast red paper; small white sentence persists.

scenes.title: The limit of words
scenes.visual: Long white word-ribbon crosses gap but stops before second person outline.

scenes.title: Final question
scenes.visual: All words recede, one cup stays, two separate figures share a small warm circle; fade to ALFAAZ.

cues.text: Have you ever opened a message, typed a few words, and then deleted them?
Maybe you only wanted to ask how someone was.
Yet even that simple question felt strangely difficult.
It is not always because we have nothing to say.
Sometimes it is because the other person carries so much meaning that an ordinary sentence suddenly feels too small.
That is the world of Alfaaz.
The word means words.
But the song keeps returning to a paradox: the more deeply we feel, the harder it can become to explain ourselves.
What if love is not only about wanting someone near you?
What if it quietly changes what you notice, what you remember, and even the person you think you are?
At first, the changes are almost invisible.
You remember how they take their tea.
You notice a particular color because they once said they liked it.
You collect stories to tell them later.
Then one day something interesting happens.
A small event occurs, and your first thought is to tell that person.
They have become part of the way you experience your own day.
Nobody announced this transformation.
There was no official beginning.
Your habits changed a little at a time, until loving someone became one of the ways you understood yourself.
But there is a question hidden in this beauty.
If another person helps shape who we become, how do we remain ourselves while loving them?
Think about a road you have walked a hundred times.
Nothing about its bricks or streetlights changes.
Yet after walking it with one particular person, the same road can feel entirely different.
A bus stop becomes a memory.
A café table becomes a small monument to a conversation.
A song played in a shop can bring back an evening you thought you had forgotten.
The objects stay ordinary.
Their meaning does not.
That may be one of the most remarkable things about affection: it changes our relationship with the world without changing the world itself.
Simone Weil called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity.
Perhaps love often begins there: in noticing what others overlook, and remembering something small because it mattered to one person.
But attention creates vulnerability.
You know how often you think about someone.
You cannot know, with the same certainty, how often they think about you.
You look at your phone again even though nothing has changed.
You wonder whether they remember the conversation you have replayed so many times.
Maybe it was extraordinary to you and ordinary to them.
Sometimes distance is not the deepest fear.
The deepest fear is discovering that a memory you have carefully kept alive has become faint in someone else.
Iris Murdoch described love as the extremely difficult realization that something other than oneself is real.
The person we love has an inner world that does not belong to us.
Their feelings may differ from ours.
Their memories may not match.
To love them seriously is to recognize that distance between us, even while wishing we could close it.
There is another unusually honest idea in Alfaaz: loving someone as much as you knew how to love.
Most of us are never formally taught how to do that well.
We learn through clumsy attempts.
Some people are good with words.
Others show care by arriving on time, listening closely, or remembering what someone needs on a difficult day.
Erich Fromm wrote that love is an activity, not a passive affect.
A powerful feeling does not automatically make us good at loving.
Care has to become something another person can experience.
You can think about someone every night and still misunderstand them.
You can speak beautifully and still fail to listen.
Sincerity matters, but what we do with that sincerity matters too.
And that brings us back to the title.
We use words to apologize, to thank people, and to say we miss them.
Yet sometimes the feeling seems much larger than the sentence.
A sentence can tell someone what you feel.
It cannot guarantee that they will feel the same thing.
Language can reach toward another person, but it cannot completely enter their inner life.
Maybe that is why Alfaaz stays with us.
We keep looking for perfect words, when love also lives in small acts of attention.
And when words are not enough, the question remains: what do we choose to do?
